introduction.text: Castel Sant’Angelo, a towering cylindrical building in Rome, was originally built as Emperor Hadrian’s mausoleum and later served as a papal fortress, prison, and museum. Its layered history and iconic silhouette make it a symbol of Rome’s imperial, religious, and cultural heritage.

history.description: Construction of Hadrian’s mausoleum on the right bank of the Tiber, begun between 134 and 139 AD.
Hadrian’s ashes, along with those of his wife Sabina and adopted son Lucius Aelius, were interred in the mausoleum in 138 AD.
Caracalla’s ashes were deposited in the mausoleum in 217 AD.
The mausoleum was converted into a military fortress in 401 AD and incorporated into the Aurelian Walls.
The Visigothic sacking of Rome in 410 AD led to the scattering of the mausoleum’s urns and ashes.
Legend of Archangel Michael appearing atop the mausoleum in 590 AD, ending the plague.
Beginning in the 14th century, the popes converted the structure into a castle.
The fortress served as refuge during the Sack of Rome in 1527.
Benvenuto Cellini was imprisoned in the castle during the 16th century.
The castle was decommissioned as a fortress and became a museum in 1901.

design.description: The building’s design features a massive cylindrical rotunda with a conical roof, originally intended as a mausoleum.
Later additions include thick walls, a moat, and a fortified corridor (Passetto di Borgo) connecting to St. Peter’s Basilica.
An ongoing project aims to create a pedestrian tunnel linking the castle to St. Peter’s Basilica beneath Piazza Pia.

art.description: A bronze statue of Saint Michael, executed by Peter Anton von Verschaffelt in 1753, crowns the castle’s roof.
An earlier marble statue of Saint Michael by Raffaello da Montelupo, created in 1536, once stood atop the castle.
The museum houses various artifacts, including the capstone of a funerary urn that once adorned Saint Peter’s Basilica.
